It mentions two discrete random variables.
It names them X and Y.
It asks about their expectations.

The question concerns the sum X plus Y.
It asks whether that sum can fail.
It allows undefined or infinite outcomes.
We should define the setting carefully.
Discrete variables take countable values.
They can be real valued here.
Finite expectation means the first moment exists.
It also means absolute integrability.
The triangle inequality then applies.
The absolute value of a sum is bounded.
That bound uses the individual absolute values.
Both individual absolute expectations are finite.
Therefore the sum expectation is finite.
No counterexample exists in this standard model.
Extended values would need special discussion.
The reference likely assumes ordinary real variables.
So the short answer is negative.
Given the reference question, the standard answer is no, because finite expectations for discrete random variables make the sum finite, and that central conclusion, under the usual definitions, in general indeed rests securely beneath the theorem.
